source.title: An Entropic Optimal Transport Loss for Learning Deep Neural Networks under Label Noise in Remote Sensing Images
source.authors: B. Damodaran; Rémi Flamary; Vivien Seguy; N. Courty

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: Tests noisy-label learning on remote-sensing datasets, a new setting. Its reported measures are test classification accuracies under structured asymmetric label noise, not the random-label fitting behavior in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own experiments with asymmetric, visually or spectrally motivated class-label flips. It does not report training error on random labels, test error at chance, or results for shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs. Its discussion of memorization in deep networks cites Zhang et al. (2017) and is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates robustness to structured label noise using clean-test accuracy, without measuring training-set memorization. It cites random-label memorization as motivation but does not test any claim version. The two-moons illustration shows a boundary enclosing mislabeled samples, without establishing perfect fitting or learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: CLEOT uses geometric structure and entropic optimal transport to improve robustness to significant label noise across aerial-scene and hyperspectral classification tasks. This summarizes their conclusion rather than establishing superiority in every table condition.
record.recipe_differences: Uses asymmetric, class-specific label flips and tests robust-loss methods in remote-sensing image classification; it does not reproduce random-label fitting experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and asymmetric noise level; the text says the effect depends on the amount of classes affected and dataset characteristics.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-entropy clean-test accuracy decreases monotonically across the reported noise settings on all four aerial datasets: 82.93 to 62.05, 89.75 to 62.25, 97.68 to 73.68, and 86.94 to 57.80 percent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Clean-test accuracy declines as selected asymmetric class-label flips increase in these remote-sensing datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: The two-moons illustration describes a complex neural-network boundary enclosing mislabeled samples after 500 epochs with label-flip probability 0.2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on partially corrupted two-moons labels can produce a boundary that accommodates mislabeled examples.

record.code_released: not stated; paper says code will be published upon acceptance
record.peer_reviewed: Computer Vision and Image Understanding (under consideration, according to the supplied text)
record.problems: No random-label condition or training-error measurements. Noise is simulated with structured asymmetric class flips, limiting comparison with claims about completely random labels. The reported baseline includes dropout, weight regularization and early stopping. Results are averages across runs with standard deviations; no significance tests are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports other methods, including CLEOT, at the same dataset and noise conditions; these were omitted because the extracted finding is the cross-entropy baseline response to asymmetric label noise, and the method comparisons do not measure random-label fitting. Table 4 results were omitted because its flattened layout makes some dataset, noise-level and value assignments ambiguous in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Random-versus-real-label fitting time and convergence speed across corruption fractions; CLEOT-versus-other-method speed claims do not measure this.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit throughout random corruption from none to all, with test error approaching chance. Reported test degradation uses selected asymmetric class flips and no training-fit measurements.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting, and whether removing regularization harms true-label generalization; no relevant ablation is reported.
Temporal ordering of shared-pattern learning and noise memorization, and differences between real- and random-label learning trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 2 cross-entropy values and clean baselines match the supplied text. Noise levels are flip probabilities for selected affected classes, not fractions corrupted across the entire dataset. Training uses frozen VGG16 features, regularization, dropout, and selection by best noisy-validation loss with early stopping. These results cannot establish either successful or failed memorization.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling or training error measurement.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed by corruption fraction.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
The paper uses structured asymmetric class flips rather than random corruption and does not report training-set fit or whether it remains perfect.
No experiment testing whether regularization prevents random-label fitting or whether its removal harms true-label generalization.
No analysis of learning order or comparison of patterns learned from real versus random labels.
